Reverence to the Buddha, whose pure mind
Made for the earth a Sun-his noble Law,
That all three worlds may follow him and reach
Salvation, who were powerless else to cross
The jungle and slough of sensuality.
To the sole Lord I bow, His Law, His Church.
Auspicious cycle of our world, adorned
By Buddhas five! Four Buddhas have arisen,
The Home of endless pity then achieved
Born as Vessantara he sought delight
In doing good to men and aye excelled
In all the Ten Perfections; passing thence
The Eye-endowed was born in Tusita,
That city where in beauty and the Ten
Who from the myriad universes came
The Paragon his observations five
In Sakiyan line. For thirty years save one
In home he dwelt, the Lord of glory; thence
He went a monk, resolved. In his desire
For highest wisdom he put forth his strength
In hard ascetic practices; he sate,
And by the high prepared path he passed
Toward wisdom's centre; there the factors four
Nor trembled, fearless as a lion maned,
He brake, affrighting them; victorious, calm
And rapt in contemplation all that night's
The lore of former births and sights occult;
Then comprehended, in the latest watch,
Inspired, the Light-giver, all duties done.
All fever cooled, and free from poison-drugs,
There was a king most wise, the lord of men,
Who loved the hearing of good Law; his name
This just and righteous ruler of the land
So truly wise with best intelligence
He ordered: "Make a pleasing lovely room,
A fragrant chamber for the mighty sage
And images of spirits." This great king
An image glorious-wonderful and fair
Might never wink,—so purely wise was he.
He copied; clad the monks with many a set
What time the gu was dedicated, fain
He fed them, cheerfully; then cried aloud
In strong desire for Buddhahood this prayer :-
This Conqueror, having plumbed the deeps of
And reached omniscience, durst not publish it
Indued with valour beyond weight!-and came:
A space of thirty yojanas, by road
To sweet Isipatana, the resort
He taught the turning of the wheel of Law,
And brahmas and immortals, all that host.
With the elder Aññakondañña he caused
To reach Nirvana, matchless path.-So I
The working of twin miracles he knew
And dealt in divers magic meet for Lords;
For from the Master's body forth there came
And dazzling rays, six coloured rays that ran
He saw and pitying brought them from all worlds
To Mt. Mèru, and ranging in one row
By magic power upon their heads he built
A jewelled path where to and fro he walked
Thereafter to the seat of Thirty Three
And gave ambrosial liquor to the hosts
So would I teach that Law inscrutable.
There on the summit of Sinèru stood
In pomp the Buddha and by power divine
Do marvels and fling open wide the world.
He taught the creatures of our earth the Law
In divers ways; by matchless Law he tamed
Who thought 'We are the Buddhas.'-So would I.
In virtue sure as earth, in fixity
As Himava, in wisdom as the heaven,
All doubt emerging, all his karma done,
By death of all his elements set free.
He tameth others, for himself is tamed;
He calmeth others, for himself is calm;
Hero without a home!-Would I were he!
In wisdom, sole. dispeller of the dark;
The poisons, lust and hate and misconceit.
Hero incomparable!—Would I were he!
As when a fisherman with subtil net
So many heretics, ill-doers, who leapt
Into the shoal of heresy beguiled
Crows and all winged fowl which cross the sky
All things both conscious and unconscious passed
The world of spirits and our world had leapt
To night and error; but that wisdom shone
And night is scattered. As the rising sun
Tamer of men, by men and spirits adored.-
Would I were such a Buddha, Charioteer,
Tamer of men, by men and spirits adored.
By this my gift, whatever boon I seek,
By this abundant merit I desire
And splendours of a monarch; nay, not even
To be the pupil of the Conqueror.
The river of Samsara, and all folk
Would speed across thereby until they reach
The Blessed City. I myself would cross
And drag the drowning over. Ay, myself
Would hatred calm. The three immoral states,
Greed, hate, delusion, rooted all in self,
O may they die, whenever born in me!
Nor yield to fire nor robbers, life by life.
Longings of sense for all delicious things,
May sense of shame, fear of reproach (declared
By the Sun's kinsman Guardians of the world)
All worldly wealth forsaking draw me near
I would fulfil hereafter, great and small,
Borne through the element the spotless moon
So I delighting in the Master's lore,
Would shine among disciples. I would know
The Master's mind, his ninefold doctrine fraught
I would do good to others and myself.
What the Great Sage forbids I would not do.
May I be alway conscious and aware
I would put forth mine energies and save
By merit of this act I would behold
Enhaloed on a rainbow pathway fair
There might I hear good Law, and bending low
And all his monks, till clad in virtues eight,
Informed by such a Teacher, I become
A Buddha in the eyes of spirits and men.
Tathagata by men and spirits adored
Would shine and be by men and spirits adored.
The twenty four infinities he saved
The fourscore and four thousand points of Law
For good of all hereafter, blazed abroad
Niccasa a ca n sento b l nam avij Set forth the transience of conditioned things
Wrecking the notion of dull fools who deemed
All things are stable,' and at last attained
The city of Nirvana, safe retreat
That city lavish of abounding bliss!"
This is the stone inscription of the king
The elements of wisdom, the Three Gems
On Sunday the fourth waxing of Kason
In the five hundred and third year to build
At an auspicious moment. That same year
On Thursday eleventh waning of Nadaw

Myanmar Text (A 39 lines, B 34, lines) tr. Charles Duroiselle (1919)
rev. Tun Aung Chain
Prosperity! Honour to the Buddha! One thousand six hundred and
twenty-eight years of the Buddha's religion having elapsed, Úri
Tribhuvanadityâdhammarâj became king in this city of Arimaddanapur. A
beloved wife of that king was named Trilokavatamsakâdevî, and that beloved
wife's son was named Râjakumâr. That king gave the beloved wife three
villages of slaves. That beloved wife having died, the king gave her
ornaments and the three villages of slaves to her son named Rajakumâr. At
the time that that king having reigned twenty-eight years, became sick even
unto death that son of the beloved wife, who was named Râjakumâr, calling
to mind the favours of the great king who had nurtured him, made an image
of the Buddha all in gold. At the time he offered (it) he spoke thus: "I, your
slave, made this golden Buddha for my lord; the three villages of slaves which
my lord gave me, I give to this golden Buddha." At that time the king, being
delighted, said: "Good, Good!" and, in the presence of the great monk
Mahather, the great monk Muggaliputtatissatther, the great monk Sumedha
the learned, the great monk Brahmapal, the great monk Brahmadiv, the great
monk Son and the great monk Sanghasena the very learned, the king poured
water. That being done, that son of the beloved wife who was named
Rajakumâr enshrined that golden Buddha, and made this cave-pagoda with a
golden spire. Having finished (it), at the time he dedicated this cave-pagoda
and Buddha, he brought up (the folk of) Sakmunalon, one village, Rapây, one
village, Henbuiw, one village, these three villages of slaves. That son of the
beloved wife, who was named Râjakumâr, poured water for this cave -
pagoda and Buddha, and thus said: “Let this deed of mine be the cause of my
obtaining Omniscience! After me, (whosoever) whether (he be) my son, or

grandson, or relative, or any other person, if he oppresses the slaves I have
offered to this Buddha, may he not behold the Buddha Arimittiyâ!"

Mon Text (A 33 lines B 46 lines) tr. C.O.Blagden (1919)
rev. Tun Aung Chain
Prosperity! Honour to Buddha! Prosperity! After the religion of the
Lord Buddha had gone on for one thousand six hundred and twenty-eight
years, in this city of Arimaddanapur King Sri Tribhuvanadityadhammarâj was
(king); one queen of that king was named Trilokavatamsakadevi; that queen's
son was named Rajakumâr. The king gave three villages of slaves to the
queen. When the queen died, the king gave all the queen's goods, together
with the three villages of slaves, to the queen's son, who was named Râjakumâr.
After the king had reigned for twenty-eight years, when the king was
sick well-nigh unto death, the queen's son, who was named Râjakumâr,
remembering the favours wherewith the king had nourished him made a golden
Buddha (and) went (and) offered it to the king, (and) addressed (him) thus:
"This golden Buddha (have) I made to assist my lord. The three villages of
slaves that my lord gave to me I am giving to this Buddha: may my lord.
approve!"
Then the king being well pleased, expressed approval, (saying), "Well
done! Well done!" Then (in the presence of) our lord the Mhather the lord
teacher Muggaliputtarissa ther, the lord teacher the learned Sumedha, the
lord teacher Brahmapal, the lord teacher Brahmadiv, the lord teacher Son,
(and) the lord teacher the very learned Sanghasena, in the presence of those
lords the king poured water onto the ground.
After this, the queen's son, who was named Rajakumar, took the golden
Buddha (and) enshrined it (and) made this golden-spired cave-pagoda. When
dedicating this Buddha (and) cave-pagoda, the queen's son brought up (the
men of) Sakmunalon, one village, Rapây, one village, Ñahhgir u(y) one
village, all those three village-communities of slaves, (and) poured out water
for the golden Buddha that he (had) enshrined in this cave-pagoda, (and)
prayed thus: "May this act of mine be a cause for the attainment (by me) of
Omniscience! Be it my child be it my grandchild, be it my kinsman, be it (any)
other person, if he do violence to the slaves whom I am giving to this
Buddha, may he not get sight of the exalted Buddha Mettey!"

on the obscure original as on the more intelligible Burmese and Mon versions).
Prosperity! 1628 years after death of the Dathagada in this city called
Rimadhanabu Sri Tribhuvanadityadhamaraja so-called was lord, his queen
consort was called Trilogavadasagâdevi, her son was called Râjagumâ (The
king) gave her three villages of slaves. When the queen had died, (he) gave
the queen's goods (and) the three villages of slaves to the queen's son
Râjagumâ.
—
When the king had reigned for twenty-eight years, (and) was sick
nigh unto death, the queen's son named Râjagumâ, [being mindful of the
benefits wherewith the king had nourished him,] caused this golden image in
the likeness of the Budha to be made, (and) brought this Budha into the
(royal) presence (and) spake thus: "This golden Budha which I have made
on my lord's behalf I present to my lord. The three villages of slaves (that)
my lord gave me I give to this sacred image of gold." Thereupon the king
was delighted (and) exclaimed, “Well done! Well done!". Then (in the
presence of) my lord Mahather, my lord Mugalubudadisathe, my lord the
learned Sumedha, my lord Vrahmaba my lord Vradeyo, my lord Su, my lord
the very learned Sagasi, in the presence of these lords of the church the king
poured water (onto the ground).
That having been done, the queen's son named Râjagumâ enshrined
the golden Budha, (and) having made the golden spire of the cave-pagoda,
pronounced the dedication of this cave-pagoda (and) having assembled (the
men of) Samanalo, one village, Rabai, one village, (and) (J)ivu one village,
these three villages of slaves, the queen's son Râjagumâ, having poured out
water to this cave-pagoda (and) Budha, spake thus: "May this that I am
doing be a cause for giving me Omniscience (and) wisdom! As for these
slaves, be it my son, be it my grandson, be it my kinsman, be it any other
person, [if he shall do violence to those that I have dedicated to this Budha,
may he never be permitted to approach the presence of] the lord Budha
Arimedeya!"

Pali Text (A 41 lines, B 40, lines) tr. Charles Duroiselle (1919)
Prosperity! Having bowed to the Buddha and other (two) Excellent
Objects, I shall relate the noble work of merit performed, in the Conqueror's
dispensation, by Râjakumâra. Hearken to me! When one thousand six
hundred and twenty-eight years had elapsed after the Nibbana of the Lord of
the World, Tibhuvanadicca, a powerful king and scion of the exalted solar
race, became king in the city called Arimaddana. He had a beloved queen,
Tilokavatamsikâ (by name), who was benevolent and skilful in all the affairs
of the king. She had a son, Râjakumâra by name, a minister, zealous in (the
management of) the affairs of state, prudent and wise. The king, graciously
disposed towards the queen, gave her three villages for her to enjoy, for life,
the revenues (accruing from) the slaves (thereof). Now, upon the death of
the queen, the king again made those three villages over to Rajakumâra. On
the king, after having ruled righteously for twenty-eight years, being seized
with a mortal illness he (Rajakumâra), remembering the numerous and great
favours of the righteous king, had a beautiful image of the Buddha made all in
gold and, carrying it with great pomp, and well pleased (with his meritorious
act), approached unto the presence of the king and told him of his intention:
"On your Majesty's behalf, I have made this beautiful golden image
of the Master; deign, my lord, to rejoice in this excellent work of
merit! The three villages which you formerly gave me, I have
dedicated to this image; at this also rejoice!"
On this being said, the king, (though) his mind was troubled by
disease, rejoiced and, pleased and delighted, exclaimed; "Good! good!" The
compassionate Mahathera, the thera Muggaliputtaka, Sumedha the wise, so
called on account of his wisdom, Brahmapala, likewise Brahmadeva the
virtuous, Sona, the learned and eminent scholar called Sanghasena:, in the
presence of these monks (the king), well pleased, poured the libation on the
ground, taking the earth to witness. Then, the minister enshrined the
beautiful golden image and built (over it) a cave-pagoda surmounted by a
golden spire. Having performed the dedication ceremony for the Buddha-
image and the cave-pagoda, he (Rajakumâra), weary of repeated birth, made
the following aspiration:
"May this meritorious work, performed and accumulated by me,
be the cause of my attaining Ommicience! Whosoever, be he my
son, or grandson, or any other relative, with evil intent and
unbelieving mind should oppress those slaves, dwellers in the three
villages, whom I have dedicated to the cave-pagoda and the golden
image of the Great Sage, may this vile person be precluded from
beholding Metteyya, the Chief of men!"
